title: He Has Risen: Emmaus, the Upper Room, and the Ascension
summary: On the first day of the week the women find Jesus' tomb empty and hear from two men in radiant clothing that he has risen. That day the risen Jesus walks unrecognized with two disciples to Emmaus, explains the Scriptures about himself, and is recognized in the breaking of bread. He then appears to the gathered disciples, shows them his hands and feet, eats before them, opens their minds to the Scriptures, commissions them as witnesses to all nations, and, blessing them near Bethany, is carried up into heaven.
story:
Everything in Luke has been moving toward Jerusalem, and here the story reaches its goal. The Jesus who was crucified and buried in chapter 23 is alive, and the chapter moves in what reads as a single day from perplexity and grief to worship and great joy. The key to the whole chapter is Scripture. The angels tell the women to remember Jesus' words; on the road Jesus shows that his suffering and glory were written in Moses and all the Prophets; in the upper room he names the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms, and says the next part of the story is also written: repentance and forgiveness of sins proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

Luke ends where he began, in the temple, with people praising God. The Gospel opened with Zechariah the priest unable to pronounce the blessing (1:21-22) and closes with Jesus lifting his hands to bless his people (verse 50), and the great joy the angel announced to the shepherds (2:10) returns in the disciples' joy (verse 52). Luke's second volume, Acts, picks up exactly here. It retells the ascension, makes clear that the appearances continued over forty days (Acts 1:3), and follows the witnesses from Jerusalem to Rome, clothed with the power from on high that Jesus promises in verse 49.
historical:
The chapter's events fall on the Sunday after the Passover at which Jesus was crucified, the Friday called the day of Preparation (23:54). The year is not fixed, but most scholars favor AD 30 or 33 (see the note on chapter 22). The first day of the week quickly became the day of Christian worship (Acts 20:7, 1 Corinthians 16:2, Revelation 1:10), a change best explained by the conviction that Jesus rose on it. The earliest written summary of the resurrection appearances is Paul's in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, from the mid-50s, which passes on a tradition he had received earlier still and which, like verse 34, puts the appearance to Peter before the appearance to the Twelve. That women were the first witnesses matters historically: Josephus says women should not be admitted as witnesses (Antiquities 4.219), and the second-century critic Celsus mocked the resurrection as resting on the word of a hysterical woman (Origen, Against Celsus 2.55).

Emmaus has several candidate sites, and none is certain. Emmaus Nicopolis (modern Imwas, near Latrun) was a well-known town where Judas Maccabeus defeated the Seleucid general Gorgias (1 Maccabees 3:40, 4:3). Eusebius identifies it as Luke's Emmaus in his Onomasticon, but it lies about 160 stadia (roughly 30 kilometers, 19 miles) from Jerusalem, which fits a variant reading in verse 13 but makes the walk there and back in one afternoon and evening hard. El-Qubeibeh, about 60 stadia northwest of the city, where the Crusaders found a Roman fort called Castellum Emmaus and where a Franciscan church now stands, and Abu Ghosh, on the road toward Jaffa, were both medieval identifications. Motza (Qaloniya), about 30 stadia west, is linked with the Emmaus where Josephus says Vespasian settled 800 veterans after the Jewish war (Jewish War 7.217). Since 2017 Israel Finkelstein and Thomas Römer, excavating at Kiriath-jearim beside Abu Ghosh, have proposed that its Hellenistic fortifications belong to the fort of Bacchides at Emmaus (1 Maccabees 9:50) and that this is Luke's village; the proposal is argued, not proven.

Bethany lay on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, about fifteen stadia (under two miles) from Jerusalem (John 11:18), and Acts places the ascension on the Mount of Olives, a Sabbath day's walk from the city (Acts 1:12). Eusebius reports that Constantine's mother Helena built a church on the Mount of Olives in memory of the ascension (Life of Constantine 3.41-43). By AD 400 Augustine could list the ascension, with the passion, resurrection, and gift of the Spirit, among the annual commemorations kept by the whole church (Letter 54.1).
cultural:
Jewish burial customs called for washing the body, wrapping it in linen, and applying spices and perfumed oils as an act of love. The women had prepared spices on Friday and rested on the Sabbath (23:56), so they came at first light on Sunday. They expected a corpse. Two men in dazzling clothing appear (verse 4); Luke's two witnesses fit the rule that a matter is established by two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and Luke has two men again at the transfiguration (9:30) and the ascension (Acts 1:10). Bowing the face to the ground was the posture of people before a heavenly being (Daniel 10:9, 10:15).

On the road, hospitality governs the scene. As evening came, travelers were urged to stay, and refusing a guest the night was shameful (Genesis 19:2-3, Judges 19:20-21). At the meal the host normally took bread, spoke the blessing, broke it, and distributed it; here the guest takes the host's part, with the same four actions Luke describes at the feeding of the five thousand (9:16) and the Last Supper (22:19), and in that familiar act they know him. ‘The breaking of the bread’ (verse 35) became Luke's phrase for the meals of the earliest church (Acts 2:42, 2:46, 20:7).

The disciples' first fear, that they were seeing a spirit (verse 37), reflects the widespread ancient belief in ghosts, the shades of the dead who might appear to the living. Jesus answers it directly: a spirit does not have flesh and bones (verse 39), and then he eats. In the book of Tobit the angel Raphael tells Tobit and his son that he did not really eat or drink but that they saw a vision (Tobit 12:19), and Jesus' eating makes the opposite point. Many Jews, following Daniel 12:2, expected God to raise the righteous dead bodily at the end of the age; no one expected the resurrection of one man in the middle of history, which is part of why the disciples were so slow to grasp what had happened. The phrase ‘the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms’ (verse 44) names the three parts of Israel's Scriptures, the Psalms standing for the Writings, a division also found in the prologue to Sirach (about 132 BC). Finally, when Jesus lifts his hands and blesses the disciples (verse 50), he acts like a priest. Aaron lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them (Leviticus 9:22), and Sirach 50:20-21 describes the high priest Simon coming out of the sanctuary and raising his hands to pronounce the blessing of the LORD over the congregation, which then bowed in worship, closely matching verses 50-53.
literary:
The chapter is a sequence of three scenes on one day: the empty tomb at dawn (verses 1-12), the road to Emmaus in the afternoon and evening (13-35), and the appearance to the gathered disciples, followed by the ascension (36-53). Each scene moves from perplexity to understanding, and each turns on remembering or opening. The women remember his words (verse 8); the Emmaus disciples' eyes are opened (verse 31) as Jesus opens the Scriptures (verse 32); the disciples' minds are opened to understand them (verse 45). Luke uses the same verb, dianoigō, in all three places. Recognition, which ancient critics since Aristotle (Poetics 11) counted among the great turning points of a story, here comes as a gift: the disciples' eyes ‘were kept’ from recognizing him and then ‘were opened’, passives that point to God as the actor.

The Emmaus story is Luke's masterpiece of irony. The risen Jesus hears his own story told as a tragedy by people who do not recognize him, and their summary is accurate as far as it goes: a prophet powerful in word and deed, condemned and crucified, a report of an empty tomb and a vision of angels. What they lack is the key, which Jesus supplies: ‘Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?’ (verse 26). Many interpreters have noticed that the story is arranged symmetrically, moving out from Jerusalem and back again, with the report that he is alive (verse 23) near its center. The word dei, ‘it is necessary’, Luke's signal of God's plan, appears three times (verses 7, 26, 44).

The chapter ties the Gospel together. It echoes the beginning, which also opened in the temple with worship, a blessing, and joy, and it gathers the Gospel's themes of hospitality and meals, the fulfilment of Scripture, the reversal of expectations, and women as faithful witnesses. It also opens Acts. Verses 47-49 compress the plan of Luke's second volume into a sentence, and the ascension is told at the end of the first book and again at the start of the second (Acts 1:9-11), a repetition Mikeal Parsons (The Departure of Jesus in Luke-Acts, 1987) studied as a deliberate hinge. In the Gospel the ascension closes Jesus' earthly story with blessing and worship; in Acts it opens the church's story with a commission and a promise of return.

outline.t: Known in the breaking of the bread
Jesus appears to the disciples in the flesh
The Scriptures opened and the witnesses commissioned

doctrines.note: Luke insists that the resurrection is bodily. The tomb is empty and the linen cloths lie by themselves (verses 3, 12); the risen Jesus has flesh and bones, bears the wounds of the cross in his hands and feet, and eats broiled fish (verses 39-43). He is not a ghost or a vision but the same Jesus, raised in a body now transformed, able to appear and vanish (verses 31, 36). His resurrection is the firstfruits of the resurrection promised to his people.

The risen Jesus teaches that Moses, all the Prophets, and the Psalms speak of him (verses 27, 44), and he opens his disciples' minds to understand them (verse 45). He does not replace Israel's Scriptures but interprets them as one story whose center is the suffering and glory of the Messiah, which is how the apostles read them in Acts.

Repentance and forgiveness of sins are to be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem, and the disciples are witnesses of these things (verses 47-48). The mission is part of what is written (verse 46), as necessary as the cross and the resurrection, and it will be carried out in the power of the Spirit the Father has promised (verse 49).

The Messiah had to suffer and then enter his glory (verse 26). The ascension (verse 51) is that entrance: the crucified and risen Jesus is taken up into heaven, where, as Peter will say, he is exalted to the right hand of God (Acts 2:33). The disciples' worship (verse 52) is the fitting response to the exalted Lord.

Jesus sends ‘the promise of My Father’ and tells the disciples to stay in the city until they are clothed with power from on high (verse 49). Acts identifies the promise as the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:4-8) and narrates its coming at Pentecost (Acts 2). The Father's promise, sent by the risen Son, empowers the witness: the shape of the church's mission is already Trinitarian.

words.note: Egeirō, to raise, rise, wake. It occurs about 144 times in the New Testament and 18 in Luke. In verse 6 the angels say ēgerthē, an aorist passive that can be rendered ‘He has risen’ or ‘He has been raised’; in verse 34 the disciples use the same form. The passive points to God as the one who raised him, and the apostles in Acts regularly say that God raised Jesus from the dead (Acts 2:24, 3:15). The New Testament also speaks of Jesus rising in his own power (verses 7 and 46 use anistēmi), and it holds the two together.

Dianoigō, to open fully. It occurs eight times in the New Testament, four of them in Luke and three in this chapter: the Emmaus disciples' eyes are opened (verse 31), Jesus opens the Scriptures to them (verse 32), and he opens the disciples' minds to understand the Scriptures (verse 45). Acts uses it of Lydia, whose heart the Lord opened (Acts 16:14), and of Paul opening the Scriptures in Thessalonica (Acts 17:3). For Luke, understanding Jesus and understanding Scripture are one gift, given by the risen Lord.

Diermēneuō, to interpret, explain, translate. It occurs six times in the New Testament: here (verse 27), in Acts 9:36 for translating a name, and four times in 1 Corinthians for interpreting tongues (12:30, 14:5, 14:13, 14:27). Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, Jesus ‘explained’ what was written about himself in all the Scriptures. The word is related to hermēneia, from which comes hermeneutics, the discipline of interpretation, and it makes the risen Jesus the church's first teacher of how to read the Old Testament.

Lutroō, to ransom, set free by paying a price, redeem. It occurs only three times in the New Testament: here, in the disciples' ‘we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel’ (verse 21), and in Titus 2:14 and 1 Peter 1:18, where Christ redeems his people by his blood. In the Septuagint it describes God's redemption of Israel from Egypt (Exodus 6:6, Deuteronomy 7:8) and from exile (Isaiah 43:1). The Emmaus disciples used it of national deliverance; the rest of the New Testament uses it of the cross they thought had ended their hope.

Klasis, breaking. It occurs only twice in the New Testament: in verse 35, where the two tell how Jesus was made known to them ‘in the breaking of the bread’, and in Acts 2:42, where the first believers devote themselves to the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers. The related verb klaō describes Jesus breaking bread at the feeding, the Supper, and Emmaus (9:16, 22:19, verse 30). Whether the Emmaus meal was eucharistic is debated, but Luke clearly connects the risen Lord's presence with the church's table.

Martus, witness. It occurs about 35 times in the New Testament, only twice in Luke but 13 times in Acts. “You are witnesses of these things” (verse 48) names the disciples' task: to testify to what they have seen and heard, above all the resurrection (Acts 1:8, 1:22, 2:32, 3:15). In the courts a witness gave evidence, and the apostles' witness rests on having been with Jesus. Because so many witnesses paid for their testimony with their lives, the word later came to mean martyr, a sense that appears on the way in Revelation (2:13, 17:6).

Epangelia, promise. It occurs about 52 times in the New Testament, once in Luke (verse 49) and eight times in Acts. ‘The promise of My Father’ is the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:4-5), and Peter's Pentecost sermon calls the Spirit the promise received from the Father and poured out by the exalted Jesus (Acts 2:33, 2:39). Paul uses the same word for the promise to Abraham fulfilled in Christ and the Spirit (Galatians 3:14). The Gospel ends pointing forward to a gift not yet given.

Anapherō, to carry up, bring up, and in sacrificial language to offer up. It occurs ten times in the New Testament. In verse 51 Jesus ‘was carried up into heaven’, an imperfect passive that pictures the ascent in process. Mark and Matthew use it of Jesus leading disciples up a mountain (Mark 9:2, Matthew 17:1), and Hebrews and 1 Peter use it of offering sacrifices and of Christ bearing our sins (Hebrews 7:27, 1 Peter 2:24). The words ‘and was carried up into heaven’ are missing from a few manuscripts (see the text note).

christ:
This chapter shows Jesus as the living Lord, the same Jesus who was crucified, now raised in a real and transformed body. His wounds are still there; he walks, speaks, breaks bread, and eats, yet he is not always recognized at first, and he appears and disappears. The church has drawn from these scenes both its confession of the bodily resurrection and its understanding that the risen body is a body made new, what Paul calls a spiritual body, not a ghost but a body fully alive to God (1 Corinthians 15:42-44).

He is the interpreter of Israel's Scriptures. The Emmaus disciples had read the promises of a redeemer (verse 21) and missed the necessity of suffering; Jesus shows them that the Messiah's road runs through the cross to glory (verse 26). Luke does not list the passages he used, but the sermons in Acts, which Luke also wrote, show which ones the church learned to read this way: the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15, Acts 3:22), the suffering Servant (Isaiah 53, Acts 8:32-35), the Holy One who does not see decay (Psalm 16:10, Acts 2:27), the Lord at God's right hand (Psalm 110:1, Acts 2:34-35), and the rejected stone made the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22, Acts 4:11). The claim is not that every verse is a prediction but that the whole story of Israel, with its law, its prophets, and its prayers, finds its center in him.

He is the host at the table and the priest who blesses. The Emmaus meal repeats the gestures of the feeding and the Supper, and Luke's readers, who broke bread in their homes (Acts 2:46), learned to look for the risen Lord there. His last act in the Gospel is to lift his hands and bless, as Aaron and the high priest Simon did (Leviticus 9:22, Sirach 50:20-21), and he departs while blessing, so that the blessing remains over his people. He is carried into heaven, and they worship him (verse 52), the first time in Luke that anyone gives Jesus the worship which he himself said belongs to God alone (4:8). The resurrection declares that Jesus' death was not defeat, that his claims were true, and that the new creation has begun; the ascension declares that the crucified one now reigns and will send the Spirit to make his witnesses bold.
interpretation:
The church's reading of this chapter began with its insistence on the physical resurrection. Ignatius of Antioch, around 110, reports that the risen Lord told Peter and those with him to take hold of him and see that he was not a bodiless demon (To the Smyrnaeans 3), a tradition close to verse 39 and aimed at Docetists, who taught that Christ only seemed to have a body. Tertullian used verse 39 against Marcion, whose own Gospel contained a form of this chapter. The Epistle of Barnabas (15.9), probably from the early second century, speaks of the eighth day on which Jesus rose and, having appeared, ascended into heaven, which some read as placing the ascension on a Sunday, as Luke's Gospel seems to. Augustine preached on Emmaus in Easter week (for example Sermon 235) and drew from it the lesson that the disciples, who failed to know Christ in the Scriptures, knew him when they practiced hospitality and broke bread; Gregory the Great's Homily 23 on the Gospels, read at Easter Monday matins for centuries, made the same point and urged his hearers to welcome strangers. Augustine also listed the ascension among the feasts kept by the whole church (Letter 54.1, around 400).

At the Reformation the ascension became a point of dispute. The Reformed tradition drew from it (verse 51, Acts 1:9-11, 3:21) the insistence that Christ's risen body is now in heaven, which shaped its teaching that believers feed on Christ by the Spirit in the Lord's Supper, while Lutherans answered that the right hand of God is not a place and that Christ's body can be present wherever he promises. Modern debate has centered on the resurrection itself (see the hard question), on the relation of Luke's Easter-day ascension to the forty days of Acts, and on the text of the chapter, where the papyrus P75 reshaped the discussion after 1961 (see the text note). The Orthodox Jewish scholar Pinchas Lapide (The Resurrection of Jesus, 1977) accepted the resurrection as a historical event while denying that it made Jesus the Messiah, a reminder that the event and its meaning can be distinguished.

The chapter is at the center of Easter worship. The Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 1-12 on Easter Day in Year C, verses 13-49 on Easter evening, verses 13-35 on the Third Sunday of Easter in Year A, verses 36b-48 on the same Sunday in Year B, and verses 44-53 on Ascension Day in every year. Emmaus is among the most painted scenes in Christian art: Caravaggio painted it twice, in 1601 (National Gallery, London) and 1606 (Brera, Milan); Velázquez set it in the background of his Kitchen Maid (about 1617 to 1618, National Gallery of Ireland); Rembrandt returned to it several times, most quietly in 1648 (Louvre); and Han van Meegeren's forged ‘Vermeer’ Supper at Emmaus, bought by the Boijmans Museum in Rotterdam in 1937, became the most famous forgery in Dutch art history. Henry Francis Lyte took the words of verse 29 for his hymn ‘Abide with Me’ (1847), written as he was dying, and T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land (1922) named the Emmaus road in its notes to the lines about the third who walks always beside you.
text:
Luke 24 is the chapter in which the text of the Gospels was most debated in the modern era. In seven places Codex Bezae (D, fifth century) and some Old Latin copies have a shorter text: they lack ‘of the Lord Jesus’ (verse 3), “He is not here; He has risen!” (verse 6), all of verse 12, Jesus' greeting ‘Peace be with you’ (verse 36), all of verse 40, ‘and was carried up into heaven’ (verse 51), in which the first hand of Sinaiticus joins them, and ‘worshiped Him’ (verse 52). Brooke Foss Westcott and Fenton John Anthony Hort (1881), who usually preferred the Alexandrian manuscripts, judged that in these places, together with Luke 22:19b-20 and Matthew 27:49, the normally expansive Western text had kept the original and the others had added. Unwilling to speak of interpolations in the manuscripts they otherwise trusted, they called the passages ‘Western non-interpolations’, and they printed the shorter text. The Revised Standard Version of 1946 and 1952 followed them.

The papyrus P75, copied around AD 200 and published in 1961, contains every one of these passages, and it agrees closely with Codex Vaticanus. Since then most editors have judged the longer text original. The Nestle-Aland text restored the passages, the RSV's second edition (1971) put back 22:19b-20 and 24:51b, and most modern translations print all of them, sometimes with notes. Klyne Snodgrass (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1972) and Michael Wade Martin (Journal of Biblical Literature, 2005) argued for the longer readings, Martin suggesting that the omissions came from scribes resisting any hint that the risen Christ's body was separate from the divine Christ. The question is not wholly closed: Mikeal Parsons (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1986) argued that P75's text shows its own Christological interest, and the SBL Greek New Testament (2010) still omits the phrases in verses 3 and 36. Some suggest the words in verse 51 were cut to avoid a clash with the forty days of Acts 1.

Other differences are smaller. In verse 13 Codex Sinaiticus and a few others read ‘one hundred sixty stadia’ for sixty, matching Emmaus Nicopolis. In verse 32 P75, Vaticanus, and Bezae lack ‘within us’. In verse 42 later manuscripts add ‘and of an honeycomb’ (KJV). In verse 47 the earliest manuscripts read ‘repentance for the forgiveness of sins’, others ‘repentance and forgiveness’. In verse 53 the earliest read ‘blessing God’, Bezae ‘praising God’, and the later Byzantine text combines them, the King James Version's ‘praising and blessing God’, a combination Westcott and Hort used as a leading example of that text's habit of joining earlier readings.

teach.big: The crucified Jesus is risen in the body, opens the Scriptures to show that his suffering and glory were God's plan, makes himself known at the table, and sends his witnesses in the Spirit's power to proclaim forgiveness to all nations.

outline.t: The empty tomb and the angels' word call faithful women to remember what Jesus said, and the first proclamation of Easter meets disbelief.
Disappointed disciples can know every fact about Jesus and still miss him; the risen Lord walks with them in their grief.
The Messiah had to suffer and then enter his glory, and all the Scriptures bear witness to him.
The risen Lord accepts hospitality, makes himself known in the breaking of the bread, and sends the two back with good news.
The risen Jesus is no ghost: he shows his wounds and eats, and our hope is the resurrection of the body.
Christ opens minds to the Scriptures and sends witnesses to all nations with repentance and forgiveness, in the power of the Father's promise.
The ascended Lord leaves his people under his blessing, and the right response is worship, joy, and praise.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first turns the resurrection into a symbol of hope or renewal and loses the body. Luke works hard to rule that out, with the empty tomb, the wounds, the flesh and bones, and the fish, and preaching should not be vaguer than the text. The second treats the Emmaus road as an allegory of every believer's inner experience and forgets that it is the testimony of named witnesses to an event. The application to our own disappointments is real, but it rests on the fact.

A third error uses verses 27 and 44 to find a hidden prediction of Christ in every Old Testament verse, or, in reaction, treats them as a mere pious device. Jesus speaks of the whole Scripture bearing witness to him, which includes promises, patterns, and prayers, and Acts shows the kind of reading he meant. A fourth pits Luke 24 against Acts 1 as though Luke did not know what he had written; the same author compresses the time in one book and spreads it out in the other. A fifth overlooks the women. They are the first to hear the news, the first to remember, and the first to proclaim it, and the apostles' dismissal of their report (verse 11) is told against the apostles. Finally, do not let the debates over whether the Emmaus meal was a Eucharist crowd out what all traditions agree on, that Christ makes himself known at the table.
teach.pastoral: This chapter will press on the grieving and on those whose hopes have died. ‘We were hoping’ (verse 21) is the prayer of many people in the room, whose marriage, child, health, or faith has not turned out as they expected. Jesus walks with the two before he corrects them, and he lets them tell the whole sad story; teachers should do the same. The chapter also meets the doubting. Luke does not hide that the apostles disbelieved the women and that even when Jesus stood among them they were frightened and could not believe for joy; doubt is treated as a stage on the way to faith, answered with evidence and presence, not with scolding. And for those who feel that God is absent, the chapter's quiet pattern, a stranger on the road, the Scriptures opened, bread broken, is the pattern of Christian worship, where the risen Lord still makes himself known.

hard.q: Did the resurrection really happen, or can it be explained another way?
hard.a:
The church confesses that Jesus rose bodily from the dead, and Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:17). The skeptic's case deserves its strongest form first. Hermann Samuel Reimarus, in fragments published by Lessing in 1778, argued that the disciples stole the body. Gerd Lüdemann (The Resurrection of Jesus, 1994) argued that Jesus' body decayed and that the appearances were visions: Peter's born of grief and guilt after his denial, Paul's of inner conflict, and the group experiences a kind of shared ecstasy. Bart Ehrman (How Jesus Became God, 2014) doubts that Jesus received an honorable burial in a known tomb, since Rome often left the crucified unburied, and holds that some disciples sincerely saw visions that convinced them he was alive. Dale Allison (Resurrecting Jesus, 2005), writing as a historian, gathered modern reports of visions of the dead, some seen by several people at once, which weakens the familiar reply that hallucinations are always private. The skeptic can also point to real differences among the accounts: Mark has one young man at the tomb, Matthew one angel, Luke two men, John two angels; the lists of women differ; Matthew and Mark point to Galilee, while Luke keeps every appearance in and near Jerusalem.

Christian scholars answer in turn. N. T. Wright (The Resurrection of the Son of God, 2003) argues that first-century Jews would not have called visions of a dead man resurrection, a word that meant a body raised, and that only an empty tomb together with appearances explains why they did. Michael Licona (The Resurrection of Jesus, 2010) argues by historians' criteria that resurrection best explains the facts most scholars grant. Both note that the early tradition in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 lists group appearances, that women as first witnesses are an odd thing to invent, that the burial by a named council member is hard to explain as fiction, and that independent accounts commonly differ in detail while agreeing on the core: the tomb found empty on the first day by women, and Jesus seen alive. Allison himself concluded that the tomb was probably found empty and that people did see Jesus after his death, while leaving the final explanation open, and the Jewish scholar Pinchas Lapide accepted the resurrection as an event without accepting Jesus as Messiah. Many who reject the resurrection do so because they judge that the dead do not rise, a conviction the evidence cannot settle by itself. Luke leaves the reader where he left the Emmaus disciples: with the Scriptures, the testimony of witnesses, and an invitation to recognize the risen one.

hard.q: Did Jesus ascend on Easter evening, as Luke 24 seems to say, or forty days later, as Acts 1 says?
hard.a:
The difficulty is plain. Luke 24 moves from the empty tomb at dawn to Emmaus in the afternoon, the return to Jerusalem that same hour (verse 33), the appearance while they were still talking (verse 36), and then, with no further time marker, the walk to Bethany and the ascension (verses 50-51). A reader naturally takes it all as one day. Yet the same author, writing to the same Theophilus, says in Acts that Jesus appeared over forty days and then was taken up from the Mount of Olives (Acts 1:3, 1:9-12). Critics have taken this as evidence that Luke's traditions were not consistent, and some have suggested that the words ‘and was carried up into heaven’ in verse 51, which the first hand of Sinaiticus and Codex Bezae lack, were added later to create an ascension the Gospel did not originally describe, or, conversely, cut to remove a clash with Acts. The Epistle of Barnabas (15.9), from the early second century, seems to join resurrection and ascension on the same Sunday, and Mikeal Parsons and Richard Pervo (Rethinking the Unity of Luke and Acts, 1993) are among those who have pressed how differently the two books tell the departure.

The responses start from Luke's own habits. He often joins events with ‘and’ or ‘then’ without marking the time between them, and verse 44 (‘Then He said to them’) and verse 50 need not follow the previous scene on the same night. The walk to Bethany and back in the dark would be a long evening after the return from Emmaus, which suggests compression. Acts 1:2 describes the first volume as covering everything until the day Jesus was taken up, which shows that Luke himself regarded the Gospel as ending with the ascension and saw no contradiction in telling it again with a time frame. Most interpreters therefore think Luke compresses the forty days in his Gospel, closing Jesus' earthly story with a single scene of blessing and worship, and spreads them out in Acts, where the forty days recall Israel's forty years and Moses' forty days, and where the risen Jesus teaches about the kingdom before the Spirit is given. Among textual critics, most now accept the words in verse 51 as original, since P75 and Vaticanus contain them, though a minority, noting Parsons's argument about P75's Christological tendency, still prefer the shorter text. Christians who hold a high view of Scripture's truthfulness are found among those who read the Gospel's ending as compressed narrative, and the confession that Christ ascended into heaven, which the creeds state, is common to both books.

observe: What do the angels tell the women to remember (verses 6-7), and how do the apostles respond to the women's report (verse 11)?
What do the Emmaus disciples say about Jesus in verses 19-24, and what is missing from their account?
What three things does Jesus do in verses 39-43 to show that he is not a spirit?
interpret: Why do you think the two disciples recognized Jesus in the breaking of the bread rather than on the road?
What does Jesus mean when he says the Messiah had to suffer and then enter his glory, and why did the disciples find that so hard to see in the Scriptures?
Why does the Gospel end with Jesus blessing his disciples and with the disciples worshiping him in the temple?
apply: The Emmaus disciples said, ‘But we were hoping.’ Where have your hopes in God seemed to end in disappointment, and what might this story say to you there?
The disciples' hearts burned as Jesus opened the Scriptures. What would help you read the Old Testament as a book that speaks of him?
Jesus sent his disciples as witnesses. To whom in your own life are you a witness of what you have seen and heard?
